1.goal: To open on what the lesson is NOT. Say out loud: there is no tense revision today.
run: The teacher's record says she has the present perfect and barely makes a grammatical error. This lesson exists because something ELSE is missing: the word order that puts the new information where the listener expects it.
If she says “but I already know grammar”, agree. She does. The object here is presentation syntax, not verb morphology.
1.expected: That she stops expecting a revision lesson.
1.support: If the distinction will not land, say one flat sentence and one cleft with the same content, and ask which one a room hears better.
1.challenge: Ask her to name a sentence she has said this week that landed badly despite being correct.
1.monitoring: Whether she treats correctness as the goal. It is not, and the whole lesson depends on that being clear from the start.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The sample starts on the next screen.
1.transition: Move on when she understands that today is not revision.

2.goal: To see what comes out BEFORE any teaching. This is diagnostic, not warm-up.
2.interaction: S says one sentence out loud; you write it down.
run: Ask her to say out loud, now, the central problem of the case from lesson 3 — one sentence.
Write the EXACT sentence down. You give it back at stage 3.
Do not correct anything here. If she produces a cleft spontaneously, note that too — it changes what the lesson has to do.
exact: The prompt, and nothing more: “In one sentence — what is the real problem with shipping in October?”
2.expected: One sentence, most likely correct and in neutral order.
2.support: If she asks which case, remind her of the model and the October launch, and nothing more.
2.challenge: Ask for a second sentence on the same problem, from the board's point of view.
2.monitoring: Whether the new information lands at the end on its own, without any prompt.
2.evidence: Her sentence, word for word. It is the material of stage 3 and the baseline of the lesson.
2.transition: Move on when you have the sentence written down.

3.goal: To put her sentence side by side with the version that carries the new information at the end.
3.interaction: T–S over the two versions, hers included.
run: Write her sentence on the screen next to version B.
Ask: do the two say the same thing? (Yes.) Which one would you hear better in a room? Let her answer.
Her sentence is probably CORRECT. Say so: the object is not error, it is effect.
3.expected: That the two carry the same content, and that only one of them puts the point where the room is listening for it.
3.support: If the difference will not come, read both out loud at the pace of a meeting and ask which one she would remember.
3.challenge: Ask her to say version B out loud and then her own again, and to name what her mouth does differently.
3.monitoring: Whether she looks for an error in her own sentence. There is none, and looking for one is the habit to interrupt.
3.evidence: How she names the difference before you give it a name.
3.transition: Move on when she points at the difference without you naming it.

4.goal: For her to name on her own what changes — the position of the new information.
4.interaction: S does the exercise alone, then T–S before the naming.
run: She does the exercise, then open the explanation.
Ask: in which of the five is the most important word the last one?
Do NOT give the name “cleft” yet. The name comes at stage 5, after she has seen the effect.
exact: Do the five say the same thing? (Yes.) Is any of them wrong? (None.) So why do two of them stay? (Because the new information lands where the listener is waiting for it.)
4.expected: The two that keep the new information at the end, marked, with a reason.
4.support: If a line resists, read it out loud twice — once flat, once with the weight at the end — and ask which one she meant.
4.challenge: Ask her to build a sixth sentence with the same content and a different ending.
4.monitoring: Whether the reason she gives is about the listener or about the rule. Only the first transfers.
4.evidence: Whether she names the position of the new information before it has a name.
4.transition: Move on when she marks the two and says why.

5.goal: To name the form, meaning and pronunciation of the three structures.
5.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S over the form.
run: She classifies, then open the explanation. Now name them: cleft, topicalization, concessive.

FORM, the two usual errors: “What the board wants IS” — the verb agrees with the whole clause, not with “board”. And “IT IS the numbers that matter” — the “it is” is fixed; it does not become “they are”.
Pronunciation: in the cleft the weight falls AFTER the “is” — what we cannot do is EXPLAIN…. If the weight falls on the “is”, the sentence sounds hesitant.
5.expected: The three named, with one job each.
5.support: If the agreement error persists, give the two versions side by side and ask which one has a clause as its subject.
5.challenge: Ask for one sentence of her own in each of the three, on the spot.
5.monitoring: Whether the weight lands after the “is”. It is what separates a cleft that lands from one that sounds unsure.
5.evidence: Whether the three are distinct for her, or blur into “emphasis”.
5.transition: Move on when she names the three.

6.goal: To produce the form out loud, with the frame on screen.
6.interaction: T gives the flat sentence; S gives it back rebuilt. Eight, at speed.
run: You give the flat sentence, she gives it back rebuilt. Eight of them, fast.
If the agreement slips, correct on the spot — here immediate correction is right, because the stage is about form.
Do not let it turn into conversation. Eight exchanges in seven minutes.
6.expected: Eight rebuilt sentences with the new information at the end.
6.support: If the frame will not come, give the first three words and let her finish.
6.challenge: Give a sentence with two candidates for the end position and ask which one she chose, and why.
6.monitoring: Agreement in the cleft, and whether the weight stays after the “is” when she speeds up.
6.evidence: How many of the eight come out without the frame on screen.
6.transition: Move on when she produces three in a row without looking at the frame.

7.goal: To move from the invented sentence to her own content.
7.interaction: S works from her own six sentences; you judge only the position.
run: She brings the six sentences from pre-class activity 6. If she has not done it, build them here — about the decision she is carrying at work this week.
The content is hers and you do not judge the content. Judge only whether the new information landed at the end.
7.expected: Four sentences of her own where the new information lands at the end.
7.support: If a sentence resists rebuilding, ask what the last word should be, and build backwards from it.
7.challenge: Ask for one of the six in all three structures, and which she would use with her own board.
7.monitoring: Whether the structure survives when the content is real and she cares about it.
7.evidence: Her four working sentences — they are the material of the production stage.
7.transition: Move on when she has four of her own that work.

8.goal: The form inside an argument, not in isolated sentences.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the room, and you disagree once.
run: She has ninety seconds to argue her own decision, using each of the three structures at least once.
You disagree once, in the middle, with the line below.
Do not correct during. Note it and hand it back at stage 9.
exact: The mid-argument disagreement, once only: “I do not think that follows. The numbers say the opposite.”
8.expected: Ninety seconds carrying the three structures, with the concessive doing the work at the objection.
8.support: If she goes silent after the objection, wait. Filling the silence removes the measurement.
8.challenge: Ask for the same argument again in forty-five seconds, keeping the concessive.
8.monitoring: THE CONCESSIVE IS THE POINT. When you disagree, the right move is to concede and hold — not to retreat, and not to repeat louder.
8.evidence: What she does at the objection: concedes and holds, retreats, or hardens. It goes in the record.
8.transition: Move on when she closes, or at ninety seconds.

9.goal: To hand back two points and to ask for the concessive again.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the board together, then one retask with two objections.
run: Two things, no more.
Then: the same argument, but you disagree twice.
Do not add new content.
exact: The retask: “Same argument — and this time I disagree twice.”
9.expected: Two concessions, each followed by a turn that keeps the point.
9.support: If the second concession gives the point away, ask what is still true after both objections.
9.challenge: Add a third objection and see whether the pattern holds or breaks.
9.monitoring: Whether, with two objections, she concedes both or hardens. Hardening is the deviation to watch.
9.evidence: What happens on the second objection. It goes in the post-lesson record.
9.transition: Move on when the two objections have been answered.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the close.
run: She ticks what she recognizes.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class asks her to rewrite two sentences from a text of her own from this month.
Announce lesson 6: it closes the block and it is timed — forty-five seconds, in the format of the TOEFL speaking task. The four lessons are read together.
exact: In the exercise the structure comes out easily. In your own text it does not — and that is where it becomes yours.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, ask which of the three structures she would use in the next meeting she has booked.
10.challenge: Ask which sentence of her own from this week she would rewrite first.
10.monitoring: A confident mark on the form with a retreat at the second objection is the gap to record. Note both together.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close.
